title: An online shop for a clothing label
metaTitle: A clothing shop built around fit
excerpt: Show fabric, fit, and the garment on a body, with measurements in text, then a short checkout. Do not build a marketplace aisle for a small label.
alt: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall. A clothing shop is that path: fabric and fit first, then a short way to pay.
caption: A path between screens, fabric and fit before payment. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What has to be on a clothing product page before the size selector?
faqs.answer: The garment on a body, the price, and enough of the cloth to judge it. Fiber, care, and garment measurements belong in text. Model height and the size they wear should sit with the images, because a flat lay alone cannot answer fit.

faqs.question: Should a clothing shop require an account?
faqs.answer: Not for a one-time purchase. Baymard's research includes shoppers who left because a site demanded an account. Let them finish as a guest, and offer to save a size after payment. A subscription or a wholesale term is a different case, and it should say so.

faqs.question: Where should returns and lead time sit?
faqs.answer: Next to the decision to buy. State the window, who pays postage, and whether made-to-order pieces are excluded, before the card. If you cut to order, the lead time belongs on the first screen with the price, not in a FAQ only.

markdown:
A clothing label ecommerce website has to show the cloth, the fit, and the garment on a body before it asks for a size and a card. The product page is that argument. Checkout is the short remainder. A marketplace grid of tiny flats and competing badges will make a small label look like a stall inside someone else's shop.

Build the page around how the piece wears. Then take payment without a second project of forms.

## Fabric, fit, and a body

The first screen shows the garment on a person, large enough that the cloth reads: weight, drape, and color. The price and the product name sit with that image, not under a promotional bar. A flat lay can follow. It should not be the only picture, because fit is the question a clothing buyer cannot answer from a folded square.

Show the movement you actually care about. A trouser needs a side and a back, not only a face-on hero. A knit needs a cuff and a neckline. A dress needs the length against a body whose height you state. If you use several models, say their heights and the size they wear, next to the images, every time. A lookbook that hides those facts is a mood, and the product page is not allowed to be only a mood.

Fabric content and care sit in text: fiber, whether it is lined, how it washes, what it cannot take. Those lines are the difference between a return and a second order. "Premium fabric" is not a fact. "100 percent wool, dry clean" is a fact. If a mill or a finish matters to how you make the piece, one sentence is enough. A paragraph of origin story can live lower. It does not replace the fiber.

Color is a variant with its own photographs. Selecting "ink" while the hero stays "bone" is how you ship the wrong expectation. Change the image with the color. If two colors are close, say so, and show them beside each other once.

## Fit without a novel

A size guide is a table, not an essay. Measurements of the garment, not only of a model body, in the units your buyers use. Chest, waist, hip, length, and the one extra measure that matters for this pattern, such as inseam or sleeve. Say whether the fit is meant to be close or easy, in a single line beside the table, so the numbers have a direction.

If you can, say how the piece compares to a size people already own. "This jacket is cut bigger than our shirt. If you are between sizes, take the smaller" is the kind of sentence that prevents a return. It has to be true for this pattern. Do not copy it onto every product because it sounded helpful on the coat.

Model measurements do not replace garment measurements. A tall model in a size small can make a short buyer order the wrong thing. Put both, and put the garment numbers where they can be found without a modal that fails on a phone.

Baymard Institute's [cart abandonment statistics](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate) are the checkout picture, and the returns line is part of fit. In that research, 13 percent of US online shoppers had abandoned a cart because the returns policy was not satisfactory, and 17 percent because checkout felt too long or complicated. A clear size table and a clear returns line do more for a label than a longer page of styling tips. State the return window, who pays postage, and whether sale or made-to-order pieces are excluded. Hide that and people either leave or order two sizes, which is its own cost.

## The collection is still your label

The category page shows the line. Same crop family, same background logic, type that belongs to the label. Do not mix a campaign photograph, a detail macro, and a ghost mannequin as three neighboring tiles. Pick the on-body crop as the thumbnail, and let details live on the product page. Mixed tiles are the unfinished look.

Filters earn their place when the catalog is large enough to need them: size, and maybe cloth or color. A twelve-piece collection does not need five filters. It needs a page you can scan. Sort by newness if you drop seasonal work. Leave "popularity" off until you have enough orders for the word to mean something. A popularity sort on a new label just freezes the first product you happened to photograph well.

Related products are the rest of the outfit you would actually suggest, limited to two or three, chosen by the label. An algorithmic rail of "similar prices" is a marketplace gesture. It pulls a buyer out of a decision and into a browse you do not have the catalog to support.

Do not carve the site into a hundred landing pages of the same shirts with different adjectives. One honest category beats ten thin ones. Google's notes on [helpful, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) are the right restraint: pages should exist because a person needs them, not because a template can stamp out another keyword. A buyer looking for the trouser should land on the trouser.

## Checkout after the size is chosen

Once the size and color are chosen, checkout asks for little. Email, delivery address, shipping method with a price and a window, payment. Baymard's average documented abandonment rate is 70.22 percent, and 42 percent of US shoppers in their study abandoned because they were browsing or not ready. Among the causes you can design, extra costs are 40 percent, a forced account is 18 percent, and not seeing the total up front is 12 percent. Show shipping before the card. If duties are likely, say that you are not collecting them or that you are, in a sentence, before payment.

Guest checkout is the default. An account can be offered after the order, to save a size or a return. A password in the middle of paying for a shirt is the forced-account problem. Baymard's ideal checkout is about 12 to 14 form elements, or 7 to 8 fields, against a US average of 23.48 elements. You can live at the short end. Phone number only if the carrier needs it.

Stock per size has to be true. Letting someone buy a small you do not have, then emailing an apology, is a broken fit conversation. If a size is gone, say so on the selector, in text, not only by fading a button. Offer a waitlist only if you will write when it returns. A waitlist that never writes is a second, quieter failure.

## After the order, and what you leave off

The confirmation repeats the size, the color, the shipping window, and the returns line. The email matches. If you made a mistake in the photograph and you know the color runs warm, do not discover that in a generated apology later. Fix the file, and if orders are already in flight, a person writes to those buyers.

Leave off countdown timers, fake low-stock counts, and reviews that do not name the size and the height of the reviewer. A review that says "love it" without a size is a compliment, not guidance. If you show reviews, show the size purchased or do not show them on the product page.

Leave off a chat that interrupts the size table. Leave off a pop-up for a discount before the garment has loaded. If you discount, do it as a visible price, not as a code the buyer must hunt. Two prices on the same shirt, one whispered, make the label look unsure.

[Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) include ecommerce design and the production front end for a shop this size. The work is the garment page and a checkout a small team can still edit, built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript rather than a theme that fights the next collection.

## Made to order and repairs

If you cut to order, the lead time is on the first screen with the price. "Ships in three weeks" belongs next to the size selector, not in a FAQ. Say whether the piece can be returned if it was cut for them. Many labels cannot accept those returns. Say that before payment, in the same plain voice as the fiber content. A surprise exception at the returns desk is how a careful buyer decides not to come back.

Repairs and alterations, if you offer them, are a page with a price or a range and a way to start. They are not a chatbot. A small label often wins loyalty here, and the page can be short. The point is that a person will see the garment again.

Wholesale and stockists, if they matter, do not share the retail checkout. A stockist list with cities is enough. A wholesale password wall that dumps buyers into the same cart with a different price is how retail customers find the other price. Keep the paths separate.

## A shop you can update when the drop lands

The next drop should be a set of fields and images, not a rebuild. Name, price, sizes, fiber, care, measurements, and the photograph set. If updating a measurement requires a developer, the size guide will go stale, and stale measurements are a fit problem you created.

Look at the category on a phone before you announce the drop. The thumbnail crop, the price, and the sold-out sizes should be readable without zooming. A desktop-only approval is how the grid looks finished in the studio and messy in the place people buy.

The photographs are the other half of this shop. [Product photography for a clothing label](/blog/product-photography-for-a-clothing-label) is next, because fabric, fit, and the body have to be shot with one crop and one background or the collection page will undo the page you just designed.
